html:
The Waimiri-Atroari, who call themselves Kinja, are a Carib-speaking people of the Amazon forest on the border of the Brazilian states of Amazonas and Roraima, north of Manaus.

For more than a century they fought off intruders: rubber and Brazil-nut gatherers, punitive expeditions and settlers. In the 1970s the military government built the BR-174 highway from Manaus to Boa Vista through their land. Clashes and epidemics cut their numbers to a few hundred by the 1980s, a toll that a Brazilian truth commission later examined. A dam and a tin mine then took more of their land. Since the late 1980s their numbers have grown again to over two thousand. Their neighbours include the Waiwai to the north.
